messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Makai still remembers the sound. Not the gunshot itself—that was muffled, almost soft—but the wet, percussive thud of the officer’s body hitting the asphalt, and then the silence that followed, broken only by the distant wail of sirens that seemed to belong to another city entirely. He had been a passenger in the patrol car, a routine ride-along arranged through a community outreach program, something he had agreed to do as a favor to his brother-in-law who worked dispatch. The traffic stop had seemed mundane until it wasn’t. The driver of the sedan had been drunk, and when the officer approached the window, the man had produced a weapon. Makai had watched it happen from twelve feet away, frozen in the back seat, the door locked. He remembers the taste of copper in his mouth, the way his vision narrowed to a tunnel, and the certainty, absolute and cold, that he was going to die in that moment. He didn’t. The officer survived, though with a shattered femur. Makai walked away physically unharmed.

That was three years ago. Now, every time the first officer steps onto the flight deck and the cabin door seals behind him, Makai feels a flicker of the same tunnel vision. It’s not the flying that gets him—the air is empty, the sky is vast, and there are no strangers leaning into his space. It’s the delays. A late fuel truck, a hold on the runway, a message from the tower that their slot has been pushed back twenty minutes—each one feels like the moment before something terrible happens. He finds himself gripping the yoke too hard, his jaw tight, scanning the horizon for something he cannot name. He has come to believe that when something takes longer than expected, it is because the universe is lining up a catastrophe. His co-pilots have noticed. They ask if he’s okay. He says he’s fine. He isn’t.

The memories come back with a force that surprises him every time. They are more real than ordinary memories—the smell of the patrol car’s vinyl seat, the exact angle of the sun through the windshield, the sound of the officer’s voice saying “stay in the car.” When these memories surface, they do not feel like the past. They feel like the present, like he is back in that back seat, and the terror is as fresh as it was then. Sometimes, the memory is so extreme that he has trouble believing it actually happened to him, as though he is recalling a scene from a movie he once watched. But that disbelief only makes the next intrusion more disorienting. The memories are triggered by ordinary things: the smell of gasoline, the weight of a seatbelt across his chest, the sensation of his stomach dropping during turbulence. Lately, even nausea from a bad meal can send him spiraling, because his body remembers the sick, hollow feeling of watching a man raise a gun.

He has started avoiding driving with people. When his ex-wife asked for a ride to the airport last month for their daughter’s flight, he told her to take a taxi. He could not explain why the thought of another person in the passenger seat made his palms sweat. He knows it is irrational, but he is certain that if he is not alone, something bad will happen—that the proximity of another body will somehow invite the same violence. At work, he has become hypervigilant in ways that are hard to hide. He startles at the clatter of a coffee cup in the crew lounge, at the sudden hiss of the cabin pressurization system, at the sound of footsteps approaching from behind. When strangers—passengers, gate agents, even the ramp crew—walk toward him in the terminal, he feels a spike of adrenaline, a readiness to defend himself that makes no sense in a brightly lit airport. He knows this, and he is embarrassed by it, but the feeling does not listen to reason.

The loop is tight now. A delay triggers a threat response, which triggers a memory, which makes him feel vulnerable again, which makes the next delay feel even more dangerous. He has started arriving at the airport two hours before his check-in just to have a buffer, but even that does not help, because the waiting itself is the problem. His performance reviews remain strong—he is a good pilot—but he has stopped volunteering for overtime, and his captain has asked if everything is all right at home. Makai said yes, because he could not say that home is where he sits in the dark, replaying a three-minute sequence of events that will not let him go. He finally sought help after a passenger with a loud cough made him flinch so badly that he nearly dropped his flight bag in front of the gate agent. He is afraid that if he does not fix this, he will lose the only job he has ever loved. He is afraid that the memory will always feel more real than the life he is living now.
